newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: First G7 envoy arrives in troubled Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: First G7 envoy arrives in troubled Cambodia.

text.p: A special envoy from the Group of Seven industrial countries arrived in Phnom Penh on Wednesday, the first of two representatives expected to express the group's concern about political chaos in Cambodia.
Claude Martin, the French Foreign Ministry's Deputy Secretary General, did not speak to reporters at Phnom Penh's airport upon his arrival.
Yukio Imagawa, a former Japanese ambassador in Phnom Penh, was due to arrive in Cambodia later on Wednesday to join Martin on the mission, a Japanese embassy official said.

The envoys arrived as political tension ran high in Cambodia due to a long-running feud between the country's two prime ministers, and as speculation mounted over the fate of Khmer Rouge guerrilla chief Pol Pot.

Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said earlier on Wednesday that he would inform the G7 envoys about Pol Pot, who was last week captured by a breakaway rebel faction in northern Cambodia.
Negotiations with the rebels on the hand-over of Pol Pot to the government were continuing, Ranariddh said.

The G7 leaders, who met with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Denver last weekend, called for an end to the political chaos and violence in Cambodia that they said threatened to shatter the relative stability since United Nations-sponsored elections in 1993.
At the end of their summit the G7 urged Cambodia's fractious leaders to "demonstrate their commitment to holding a free and fair elections by setting a specific date".
Ranariddh announced on Tuesday that he and his partner in the country's uneasy ruling coalition, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, had agreed that Cambodia's next general election would be in May.
Ranariddh's royalist party won the 1993 election but agreed to form the coalition with Hun Sen after he questioned the election results.
Hun Sen led the communist government which ruled the country prior to the U.N.-organised peace process.
Relations between the two premiers deteriorated sharply last year after Ranariddh demanded that he be given a greater share of power to govern in the provinces.
Their dispute has deadlocked government. The national assembly was unable to reconvene in April as scheduled, preventing the passing of key legislation, including electoral laws.
Last week bodyguards loyal to the two prime ministers fought a gun battle on the streets of the capital which left two of Ranariddh's men dead.
The leaders played down the clash as an isolated incident but analysts said it illustrated the deep animosity between the two sides and the potential for more violence.
The disintegrating Khmer Rouge guerrilla force has also become a key issue of contention between the two with both men seeking political advantage as the group splits up.
